questions.solution:
Final a depends only on which a-update runs first; final b only on which b-update runs first.
- a: [latex](1+1)\times2=4[/latex] if T1's update is first, [latex]2\times1+1=3[/latex] otherwise.
- b: [latex](1+1)\times2=4[/latex] if T1's update is first, [latex]3[/latex] otherwise.

- T1 then T2: (4, 4). T2 then T1: (3, 3).
- T1: a=a+1, T2: b=2b, T2: a=2a, T1: b=b+1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] (4, 3).
- (3, 4) is impossible: it needs T2's a-update before T1's a-update and T1's b-update before T2's b-update. But in program order T1 does a before b and T2 does b before a, so this creates a cycle.

Answer: (a=4, b=4); (a=3, b=3); (a=4, b=3)

questions.text: Which of the following process state transitions is/are NOT possible?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Running [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Ready: possible (preemption / time slice over).
- Waiting [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Running: NOT possible. When the I/O finishes, the process goes to Ready; only the scheduler can move it to Running.
- Ready [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Waiting: NOT possible. A process can block (request I/O) only while it is running.
- Running [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Terminated: possible (exit).

Answer: Waiting to Running, Ready to Waiting

questions.text: Which of the following statements about threads is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Threads can also be implemented in user space (user-level threads) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- The file descriptor table belongs to the process and is shared by all its threads [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Every thread has its own stack (and registers, PC) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Threads share the same address space, so one thread can read/overwrite another thread's data; there is no protection between them [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Threads belonging to a process are by default not protected from each other

questions.text:
Consider a computer system with 57-bit virtual addressing using multi-level tree-structured page tables with L levels for virtual to physical address translation. The page size is 4 KB (1 KB = 1024 B) and a page table entry at any of the levels occupies 8 bytes.
The value of L is ______.
questions.solution:
Page size 4 KB [latex]=2^{12}[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 12 offset bits. VPN bits [latex]=57-12=45[/latex].

One page-table page holds [latex]\frac{4096}{8}=512=2^9[/latex] entries [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] each level resolves 9 bits.

Levels [latex]L=\frac{45}{9}=5[/latex]

Answer: 5

questions.text:
Consider the following two-dimensional array D in the C programming language, which is stored in row-major order:

int D[128][128];

Demand paging is used for allocating memory and each physical page frame holds 512 elements of the array D. The Least Recently Used (LRU) page-replacement policy is used by the operating system. A total of 30 physical page frames are allocated to a process which executes the following code snippet:

for (int i = 0; i < 128; i++)
       for (int j = 0; j < 128; j++) 
                   D[j][i] *= 10;

The number of page faults generated during the execution of this code snippet is _____.
questions.solution:
One page = 512 ints = 4 rows of D (each row has 128 ints). D has 128 rows [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 32 pages.

The loop accesses D[j][i] column-wise: for each i, j goes 0 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 127, touching all 32 pages in order (one page per 4 rows).

With 30 frames and LRU, cycling through 32 pages means each page is evicted before it is needed again. So every new page in each pass faults: 32 faults per value of i.

Total [latex]=128\times32=4096[/latex]

Answer: 4096
